regions.title: Commitments & governing law
regions.description: Identify the undertaking and the body of law that applies.
regions.routeLabel: What was promised, and which law applies?
regions.why: The entrance: centred above the formation core so the reader starts with "what was promised, and which law applies" before the four formation questions below.

regions.title: Consideration
regions.description: Move from the requested exchange to its sufficiency and limits.
regions.routeLabel: Was the promise bargained for?
regions.why: Bottom-left of the core, on the west side so its two substitutes (reliance, formalities) sit right beside it as alternatives.

regions.title: Reliance & restitution
regions.description: Distinguish induced changes of position from benefits received.
regions.routeLabel: If not, did someone rely on it, or get enriched?
regions.why: West column, level with consideration (6 shared connections): the other route when no bargain exists; remedies sits directly below it (9 connections on protected interests).

regions.title: Assent & intent
regions.description: Examine the communicated agreement, context, and notice.
regions.routeLabel: Did the parties actually agree?
regions.why: Bottom-right of the core and the hub of the map: interpretation (16), terms (15), bargaining (10) and limits (10) all sit within one step of it.

regions.title: Offer
regions.description: Find the offer, then determine how long it can be accepted.
regions.routeLabel: Was there an offer, and is it still open?
regions.why: Top-left of the formation core; the first of the two mutual-assent questions, read left to right into acceptance (12 shared connections).

regions.title: Acceptance
regions.description: Identify the responsive act, the invited method, and its timing.
regions.routeLabel: Was it accepted, how, and when?
regions.why: Top-right of the core, beside offer and directly above assent; flows on to Terms & battle of forms, the formation-by-forms sequel to acceptance.

regions.title: Formalities
regions.description: Separate substitutes for consideration from writing requirements.
regions.routeLabel: Does a writing or a seal matter?
regions.why: West column, level with the offer row: a seal or writing as a stand-in for consideration, so it faces the core from outside it.

regions.title: Terms & battle of forms
regions.description: Separate whether a contract formed from which terms belong to it.
regions.routeLabel: Which terms made it in when forms clash?
regions.why: East of the core, level with acceptance: which terms made it in is the last formation question and the first content question.

regions.title: Remedies
regions.description: Choose the protected interest, then examine the form of relief.
regions.routeLabel: What can the injured party get?
regions.why: Bottom-left, under reliance (9 connections on the protected interests) and beside its own detail region.

regions.title: Study workbench
regions.description: Keep broad lenses, reading records, and source-tracking notes out of the doctrinal route.

regions.title: Negotiations & incomplete agreements
regions.description: Explore the questions, then read the cases and their course-wide connections.
regions.routeLabel: Is an unfinished deal a deal?
regions.why: Eastern edge, top: unfinished deals mark the boundary of the bargain; adjacent to interpretation (17) and above limits (10).

regions.title: Modifying & policing agreement
regions.description: Explore the questions, then read the cases and their course-wide connections.
regions.routeLabel: Can the deal be changed, and was it fairly made?
regions.why: Lower band, directly beneath interpretation and diagonal to assent: modification and defective consent police a bargain that already exists.

regions.title: Interpreting the agreement
regions.description: Explore the questions, then read the cases and their course-wide connections.
regions.routeLabel: What do the words mean, and what evidence counts?
regions.why: East of assent (16 connections), the centre of the content zone; negotiation (17) is next door and performance sits diagonally below.

regions.title: Limits on contractual terms
regions.description: Explore the questions, then read the cases and their course-wide connections.
regions.routeLabel: Which terms will the law refuse to enforce?
regions.why: Eastern edge, below negotiation: terms the law refuses to enforce belong at the boundary, one step from assent and interpretation.

regions.title: Performance & conditions
regions.description: Explore the questions, then read the cases and their course-wide connections.
regions.routeLabel: Who had to perform first, and did they?
regions.why: Lower band under the core, next to the costs zone: "did they perform?" is the hinge between the contract in force and what breach costs.

regions.title: Measuring and limiting relief
regions.description: Explore the questions, then read the cases and their course-wide connections.
regions.routeLabel: How is that measured, and where does it stop?
regions.why: Bottom-left beside remedies (11) and one gap from performance (6): measurement and limits of relief are the terminus of the flow.

regions.title: Mistaken assumptions & changed events
regions.description: Explore the questions, then read the cases and their course-wide connections.
regions.routeLabel: Does mistake or a changed world excuse performance?
regions.why: Lower band, eastern end under limits: mistake and changed circumstances are the last escape before liability.

regions.title: Third-party rights & transfers
regions.description: Explore the questions, then read the cases and their course-wide connections.
regions.routeLabel: Who else can enforce or take over the deal?
regions.why: Top-right corner, outside every zone: people beyond the original parties sit literally beyond the bargain, above the boundary column.

regions.title: Semester source and reading records
regions.description: Explore the questions, then read the cases and their course-wide connections.
regions.why: Top-left corner margin, outside every zone: reading records are bookkeeping, kept next to "Start here" but out of the subject structure.

regions.title: The civil action and its legal framework
regions.description: Which court, which law, and which procedural question?
regions.routeLabel: What is a civil action, and what governs it?
regions.why: Entry point at the top-left corner, where reading begins; it sits above governing law (14 links) and beside personal jurisdiction (15 links).

regions.title: Authority over defendants
regions.description: Identify the defendant’s forum connection or another recognized basis.
regions.routeLabel: Can this court reach the defendant?
regions.why: First and tallest gate of the threshold band, standing on the threshold line; the landmarks hang directly beneath it (61 links).

regions.title: Notice, service, and hearing
regions.description: Explain how an affected person learns of the suit and can respond.
regions.routeLabel: Was the defendant told, and heard?
regions.why: Second gate, right of personal jurisdiction (14 links): once the court can reach the defendant, it must tell him.

regions.title: Federal subject-matter jurisdiction
regions.description: Identify original power, related claims, and the route from state court.
regions.routeLabel: Can a federal court hear this kind of case?
regions.why: Third gate: which kind of court; placed above joinder and class actions so supplemental jurisdiction and CAFA ribbons stay short.

regions.title: Venue and movement between courts
regions.description: Separate a proper location from a more suitable location.
regions.routeLabel: Which district, and can the case move?
regions.why: Last and smallest gate at the right end of the band: which district, and whether the case can move.

regions.title: Ascertaining the applicable law
regions.description: Identify the competing state and federal sources before selecting a test.
regions.routeLabel: Whose law applies in federal court?
regions.why: First stage of the chamber, directly beneath the framework: the suit is in federal court, so whose law applies comes first.

regions.title: Modern pleading
regions.description: Move from an intelligible claim to responses, amendment, and responsible filings.
regions.routeLabel: What must the complaint and answer say?
regions.why: Second stage: what the complaint and answer say; sits beneath the root and beside governing law.

regions.title: Joinder and coordinated litigation
regions.description: Identify who claims against whom, the procedural device, and independent authority.
regions.routeLabel: Who and what can be joined in one action?
regions.why: Third stage: who and what is in the action; diagonal from subject-matter jurisdiction for the supplemental-jurisdiction links (8).

regions.title: Class actions
regions.description: Representation, certification, notice, settlement, and the effect on absentees.
regions.routeLabel: When can one suit bind a class?
regions.why: Fourth stage, joinder scaled up; directly beneath subject-matter jurisdiction (7 links) and beside joinder (5 links).

regions.title: Summary judgment
regions.description: Connect the evidence, burdens, and permissible factfinding.
regions.routeLabel: Can the case end before trial?
regions.why: Terminus at the right end of the chamber: the suit flows left to right toward judgment.

regions.title: Legislative process and statutory interpretation
regions.description: Legislative process and statutory interpretation in the assigned readings.
regions.routeLabel: How statutes are made and read
regions.why: Top of the Congress pillar: the course starts where statutes start, and the 44 ribbons to the Katzmann continuation stay a single vertical step.

regions.title: Delegation and statutory authority
regions.description: Delegation and statutory authority in the assigned readings.
regions.routeLabel: How much power can Congress hand over?
regions.why: Foot of the Congress pillar, level with the agencies row: the hand-off from Congress to agencies is the arrow that leaves this box to the right.

regions.title: Appointments and executive structure
regions.description: Appointments and executive structure in the assigned readings.
regions.routeLabel: Who may hold federal office, and who appoints them?
regions.why: Left end of the President row, nearest Congress, because Buckley, Freytag and Arthrex are fights over which branch staffs the executive.

regions.title: Removal and agency independence
regions.description: Removal and agency independence in the assigned readings.
regions.routeLabel: Who can fire them?
regions.why: Beside appointments (4 ribbons) and above rulemaking; the delegation-to-removal diagonal is the Congress-versus-President contrast.

regions.title: Presidential control
regions.description: Presidential control in the assigned readings.
regions.routeLabel: How does the President direct the agencies?
regions.why: Right end of the President row, touching the courts column and above notice-and-comment rulemaking: Youngstown and executive-order review sit where presidential power meets judicial review (3 ribbons).

regions.title: Guidance and exceptions to notice and comment
regions.description: Policy statements, interpretive rules and procedural exceptions; related review connections retain their individual explanations.
regions.routeLabel: When may an agency skip notice and comment?
regions.why: Centre of the agencies row, where delegated power arrives and where the row's ribbons to judicial review and deference are balanced.

regions.title: Judicial review
regions.description: Judicial review in the assigned readings.
regions.routeLabel: When courts review agency action
regions.why: Middle of the courts pillar, level with the agencies row and touching administrative rulemaking, so its ribbons to the agency regions, standing and deference stay short.

regions.title: Judicial review and standing
regions.description: Judicial review and standing in the assigned readings.
regions.routeLabel: Who may bring the challenge?
regions.why: Base of the courts pillar: the threshold question sits at the foundation of judicial review, adjacent to it (6 ribbons).

regions.title: Administrative adjudication
regions.description: Administrative adjudication in the assigned readings.
regions.routeLabel: How agencies decide individual cases
regions.why: Left of the agencies row, under appointments: ALJs are the officers of Lucia, Arthrex and Jarkesy, and the rule-or-order contrast with rulemaking is one step right.

regions.title: Administrative rulemaking
regions.description: Administrative rulemaking in the assigned readings.
regions.routeLabel: Notice, comment and the record
regions.why: Right end of the agencies row, touching judicial review (10 ribbons, the course's densest cross-region link) and beneath presidential control's regulatory review.

regions.title: Judicial review of agency interpretation
regions.description: Judicial review of agency interpretation in the assigned readings.
regions.routeLabel: How much deference agencies get
regions.why: Top of the courts pillar, level with the statutory-interpretation region across the map: Chevron, Loper Bright and Skidmore are interpretation seen from the bench.

regions.title: Reading plans and sources on file
regions.description: Reading plans and the sources on file for the assigned readings.
regions.why: Bookkeeping, tucked in the empty bottom margin beneath the agencies block, right-aligned to the courts base and outside every zone.

Contracts.concept: Contracts is organised around one question, what makes a promise a contract, so the map is built as a core with an orbit. The four formation subjects (offer, acceptance, consideration, assent) form a tight 2x2 block at the centre, entered from 'Start here' (Commitments & governing law) directly above it. Everything else is placed by its relation to that core and by the ribbons it shares with it. West of the core, level with consideration, sit the two substitutes for a bargain (reliance and restitution; formalities), read as 'or' alternatives. East of the core, level with assent, sits the content of the bargain (terms, interpretation), and beyond it, at the eastern edge, the boundary of the bargain (unfinished deals; terms the law refuses). Third parties float alone in the top-right corner, literally beyond the parties. A horizontal moat of empty space separates 'forming' above from 'the contract in force' below: performance, modification and policing, and excuses run under the core, and the costs of breach (remedies, measuring relief) close the loop at the bottom-left under reliance, whose protected-interest cases they share. Reading order is a clockwise loop, start to core to content to force to cost; the heaviest connection pairs (interpretation-negotiation 17, assent-interpretation 16, assent-terms 15, offer-acceptance 12, remedies-depth 11) are all adjacent. The semester workbench is tucked in the top-left margin outside every zone.

Civil Procedure.concept: Civil Procedure is drawn as two horizontal bands facing each other across a gutter. The upper band, 'Can this court hear it?', is a skyline of four gates (authority over the defendant, notice, federal subject-matter jurisdiction, venue) standing left to right on one straight threshold line; each gate's height is its doctrinal depth, so personal jurisdiction towers at the left. The framework region sits at the top-left corner as the entry point, outside both bands. Hanging from the threshold line directly beneath personal jurisdiction, in the gutter, are the earlier jurisdiction landmarks: the historical root (Pennoyer to Shoe) from which the tallest gate grew, deliberately un-zoned so it reads as origin rather than as a stage. The lower band, 'The life of the suit', hangs from a single top line and flows left to right toward judgment: governing law (with the Berk v. Choy extension attached beneath it) under the framework, then pleading, joinder, class actions, and summary judgment as the terminus at the right edge. Columns align vertically where doctrine connects: the framework over Erie, subject-matter jurisdiction over joinder and class actions (supplemental jurisdiction, CAFA), so the ribbons between bands are short and mostly vertical. Two 'depends' spines from subject-matter jurisdiction down to Erie and to joinder show that the chamber rests on the gates; the flow spines trace the plaintiff's route.

Legislation and the Regulatory State.concept: The map is the separation-of-powers frame with the agencies caught inside it. Two tall pillars bound the course: on the left Congress (the statute is made at the top, read through Katzmann's methods beneath, and handed over to agencies at the foot), on the right the courts (how they read statutes at the top, judicial review in the middle level with the agencies it polices, standing as the foundation). Between the pillars sits the executive as two stacked rows: the President and the officers above (appointments nearest Congress, presidential control nearest the courts, removal in the middle where the two political branches fight over independence), and directly beneath them the agencies doing their work (adjudication under the appointments cases about its judges, rulemaking in the centre, notice-and-comment against the courts), so the vertical axis inside the executive literally reads as control from above. The horizontal axis is the life of a statute, statute to agency to court, and the syllabus survives as a reading path (steps 1-2 down the left pillar, 3-5 across the top row, the agencies row, 9-11 down the right pillar). Heavily connected pairs are adjacent: the interpretation continuation under its parent (44 ribbons), judicial review level with the agencies row and touching notice-and-comment rulemaking (10), presidential control against judicial review, appointments against removal. Spine lines mark the three inter-branch tensions (Congress vs President over delegation and removal, President vs courts, courts reading statutes with Congress's tools) and the flows down and across. The bookkeeping region sits alone in the bottom margin under the agencies, outside every zone.

audit.scope: Every effective core graph node, region and district screened for topic placement; all map geometry checked mechanically. Native authority, dictionary term and SCOTUS entry layouts are private navigation surfaces, not graph homes, and share the global drag lock.
audit.preserved: All account prose, original sources and connection records. Distinct legacy accounts are co-located, not deleted or silently merged.
audit.limitations: Doctrinal proximity is a study classification, not an assertion that each neighboring authority adopts the same rule. No new legal relationship is inferred from layout.

regionReviews.title: Commitments & governing law
regionReviews.rationale: The entrance: centred above the formation core so the reader starts with "what was promised, and which law applies" before the four formation questions below.

regionReviews.title: Consideration
regionReviews.rationale: Bottom-left of the core, on the west side so its two substitutes (reliance, formalities) sit right beside it as alternatives.

regionReviews.title: Reliance & restitution

regionReviews.title: Formalities

regionReviews.title: Remedies

regionReviews.title: Interpreting the agreement
